Both are designed to handle the deterministic and also the stochastic setting, and both are enhanced with bespoke variance-reduction techniques for better theoretical and practical performance. Due to space restrictions, we only describe MASHA1 in the main body of the paper, and relegate MASHA2 and the associated theory to Appendix B. ### 2.3 THEORETICAL COMPLEXITY RESULTS We establish a number of theoretical complexity results for our methods, which we summarize in Table 2. We consider the strongly convex - strongly concave regime as well as the more general convex - concave regime. In the first case we obtain linear convergence results $\left( {O\left( {\log 1/\epsilon }\right) }\right)$ in terms of the distance to solution, and in the latter we obtain fast sublinear convergence results $\left( {O\left( {1/\epsilon }\right) }\right)$ in terms of the gap function. The rates for MASHA1 improve with the number of clients $M$ and have weak dependence on the conditioning of the problem. ## 3 Problem Formulation and Assumptions Let us first introduce basic notation. We write $\langle x, y\rangle \mathrel{\text{:=}} \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{d}{x}_{i}{y}_{i}$ to denote the standard Euclidean inner product of vectors $x, y \in {\mathbb{R}}^{d}$ . This induces ${\ell }_{2}$ -norm in ${\mathbb{R}}^{d}$ as usual: $\parallel x\parallel \mathrel{\text{:=}} \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle }$ . We also introduce the proximal operator, defined as ${\operatorname{prox}}_{g}\left( z\right) \mathrel{\text{:=}} \arg \mathop{\min }\limits_{{u \in \mathcal{Z}}}\left\{ {g\left( u\right) + \frac{1}{2}\parallel u - z{\parallel }^{2}}\right\}$ , which is well defined for proper lower semicontinuous convex functions $g : {\mathbb{R}}^{d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \cup \{ + \infty \}$ . ### 3.1 Problem FORMULATION We study distributed variational inequality (VI) problems of the form $$ \text{Find}{z}^{ * } \in \mathcal{Z}\text{such that}\left\langle {F\left( {z}^{ * }\right) , z - {z}^{ * }}\right\rangle + h\left( z\right) - h\left( {z}^{ * }\right) \geq 0,\;\forall z \in \mathcal{Z}\text{,} \tag{3} $$ where $\mathcal{Z}$ is a nonempty closed convex subset of ${\mathbb{R}}^{d}, F : {\mathbb{R}}^{d} \rightarrow {\mathbb{R}}^{d}$ is an operator with certain favorable properties (e.g., Lipschitzness and monotonicity), and $h : {\mathbb{R}}^{d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \cup \{ + \infty \}$ is a proper lower semicontinuous convex function. We assume that the training data describing $F$ is distributed across $M$ workers/nodes/clients $$ F\left( z\right) \mathrel{\text{:=}} \frac{1}{M}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{m = 1}}^{M}{F}_{m}\left( z\right) \tag{4} $$ where ${F}_{m} : {\mathbb{R}}^{d} \rightarrow {\mathbb{R}}^{d}$ for all $m \in \{ 1,2,\ldots , M\}$ , and for some results we further assume that ${F}_{m}$ is of a finite-sum structure as well: $$ {F}_{m}\left( z\right) \mathrel{\text{:=}} \frac{1}{r}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{r}{F}_{m, i}\left( z\right) . \tag{5} $$ ### 3.2 ASSUMPTIONS Next, we list two key assumptions - both are standard in the literature on VIs. Assumption 1 (Lipschitzness in mean) For all clients $m = 1,2,\ldots , M$ , the operator ${F}_{m}\left( z\right)$ : ${\mathbb{R}}^{d} \rightarrow {\mathbb{R}}^{d}$ is Lipschitz in mean with constant ${L}_{m} \geq 0$ on $\mathcal{Z}$ . That is, $$ \frac{1}{r}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{r}{\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{m, i}\left( {z}_{1}\right) - {F}_{m, i}\left( {z}_{2}\right) \end{Vmatrix}}^{2} \leq {L}_{m}^{2}{\begin{Vmatrix}{z}_{1} - {z}_{2}\end{Vmatrix}}^{2},\;\forall {z}_{1},{z}_{2} \in \mathcal{Z}. \tag{6} $$ For problem (4), Assumption 1 is to be interpreted to hold with $r$ is equal 1, i.e., with ${F}_{m} = {F}_{m,1}$ . Assumption 2 (Monotonicity and convexity) (SM) Strong monotonicity/strong convexity. There exist non-negative constants ${\mu }_{F},{\mu }_{h}$ such that ${\mu }_{h} + {\mu }_{F} > 0$ , and the following statements hold: $$ \left\langle {F\left( {z}_{1}\right) - F\left( {z}_{2}\right) ,{z}_{1} - {z}_{2}}\right\rangle \geq {\mu }_{F}{\begin{Vmatrix}{z}_{1} - {z}_{2}\end{Vmatrix}}^{2},\;\forall {z}_{1},{z}_{2} \in \mathcal{Z}, \tag{7} $$ $$ h\left( {z}_{1}\right) - h\left( {z}_{2}\right) - \left\langle {\nabla h\left( {z}_{2}\right) ,{z}_{1} - {z}_{2}}\right\rangle \geq \frac{{\mu }_{h}}{2}{\begin{Vmatrix}{z}_{1} - {z}_{2}\end{Vmatrix}}^{2},\;\forall {z}_{1},{z}_{2} \in \mathcal{Z}. \tag{8} $$ (M) Monotonicity/convexity. $$ \left\langle {F\left( {z}_{1}\right) - F\left( {z}_{2}\right) ,{z}_{1} - {z}_{2}}\right\rangle \geq 0,\;h\left( {z}_{1}\right) - h\left( {z}_{2}\right) - \left\langle {\nabla h\left( {z}_{2}\right) ,{z}_{1} - {z}_{2}}\right\rangle \geq 0,\;\forall {z}_{1},{z}_{2} \in \mathcal{Z}. \tag{9} $$ ## 4 MASHA1: HANDLING UNBIASED COMPRESSORS In this section we present only one of our two new algorithms: MASHA1 (Algorithm 1) - the method that relies on unbiased compressors. Due to lack of space, we include MASHA2 (Algorithm 2) - the method that relies on contractive compressors in the appendix. Both algorithms are presented for two modes: deterministic (4) and stochastic (4)-(5). We denote the lines related to the deterministic regime in blue, and in red - to the stochastic one. Black lines are common to both modes. ### 4.1 THE ALGORITHM MASHA1 is a modification of the extra-step method. At the beginning of each iteration of Algorithm 1, each device knows the value of $F\left( {w}^{k}\right)$ , hence it can calculate ${\bar{z}}^{k}$ and ${z}^{k + 1/2}$ locally. Then it sends the compressed version of the difference ${F}_{m}\left( {z}^{k + 1/2}\right) - {F}_{m}\left( {w}^{k}\right)$ to the server, and the server does a reverse compressed broadcast. As a result, an unbiased estimate of ${F}_{m}\left( {z}^{k + 1/2}\right) - {F}_{m}\left( {w}^{k}\right)$ appears on each node. Then, all devices make a final update on ${z}^{k + 1}$ , and also update the ${w}^{k + 1} = {z}^{k + 1}$ point if the ${b}_{k} = 1$ or save it from the previous iteration ${w}^{k + 1} = {w}^{k}$ . In the case when the point ${w}^{k + 1} = {z}^{k + 1}$ , we need to exchange the full values of ${F}_{m}\left( {w}^{k + 1}\right)$ so that at the beginning of the next iteration the value of $F\left( {w}^{k + 1}\right)$ is known to all nodes. In the stochastic case, Algorithm 1 has the same form, the only thing that changes is that one need to generate a function number (batch number) from 1 to $r$ . We use a possibly difference compressor on each device and also on the server. To distinguish between them, we will use the following notation: ${Q}_{m}^{\text{dev }},{q}_{m}^{\text{dev }},{\beta }_{m}^{\text{dev }}$ and ${Q}^{\text{serv }},{q}^{\text{serv }},{q}^{\text{serv }}$ Note that, if $Q$ is the identity quantization, i.e., $Q\left( x\right) = x$ , then MASHA1 is a distributed analogue of the method from Alacaoglu & Malitsky (2021). It is important to note main differences from minimization problems. For minimization problems, compressed gradient methods are constructed on the gradient descent or the accelerated gradient descent methods. Here, the extragradient method is taken as a basis. In the experiments, we will see the importance of this fact, i.e., gradient descent type methods will diverge even on simple problems. The second key difference is that we need not compress ${F}_{m}\left( {z}^{k + 1/2}\right)$ itself, but the difference ${F}_{m}\left( {z}^{k + 1/2}\right) - F\left( {w}^{k}\right)$ . We will also see the importance of this approach in the experiments. The later idea is similar to the approach used in the DIANA, VR-DIANA (Mishchenko et al., 2019; Horváth et al., 2019), MARINA (Gorbunov et al., 2021) and EF21 (Richtárik et al., 2021) methods in optimization. Our analysis relies on the following Lyapunov function: $$ {V}_{k} \mathrel{\text{:=}} \tau {\begin{Vmatrix}{z}^{k} - {z}^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}^{2} + {\begin{Vmatrix}{w}^{k} - {z}^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}^{2}, \tag{10} $$ This criterion is used in the strongly monotone case. For the general monotone case, another convergence criterion is used - the gap function: $$ \operatorname{Gap}\left( z\right) \mathrel{\text{:=}} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{u \in \mathcal{C}}}\left\lbrack {\langle F\left( u\right) , z - u\rangle + h\left( z\right) - h\left( u\right) }\right\rbrack . \tag{11} $$ Here we do not take the maximum over the entire set $\mathcal{Z}$ (as in the classical version), but over $\mathcal{C} - \mathrm{a}$ compact subset of $\mathcal{Z}$ . Thus, we can also consider unbounded sets $\mathcal{Z}$ . This is permissible, since such a version of the criterion is valid if the solution ${z}^{ * }$ lies in $\mathcal{C}$ ; for details see the work of Nesterov (2007). Theorem 1 (Convergence of MASHA1) Let Assumption 1 be satisfied. Then, if one of cases from Assumption 2 is additionally fulfilled, the following estimates hold for the iterates of MASHA1: - for strongly-monotone/convex case with stepsize $0 < \gamma \leq \min \left\{ {\frac{\sqrt{1 - \tau }}{4{C}_{q}};\frac{1 - \tau }{4\left( {{\mu }_{F} + {\mu }_{h}}\right) }}\right\}$ and ${C}_{q} \mathrel{\text{:=}}$ $\sqrt{\frac{{q}^{\text{serv }}}{{M}^{2}}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{m = 1}}^{M}\left( {{q}_{m}^{\text{dev }} + M - 1}\right) {L}_{m}^{2}}$ : $$ \mathbb{E}\left\lbrack {V}_{K}\right\rbrack \leq {\left( 1 - \gamma \cdot \frac{{\mu }_{F} + {\mu }_{h}}{16}\right) }^{K - 1} \cdot {V}_{0}, $$ - for monotone/convex case with $\gamma \leq \frac{\sqrt{1 - \tau }}{4{C}_{q}}$ : $$ \mathbb{E}\left\lbrack {\operatorname{Gap}\left( {\bar{z}}^{K}\right) }\right\rbrack \leq \frac{8\mathop{\max }\limits_{{u \in c}}\left\lbrack {\begin{Vmatrix}{z}^{0} - u\end{Vmatrix}}^{2}\right\rbrack }{\gamma K},\;\text{ where }\;{\bar{z}}^{K} = \frac{1}{K}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 0}}^{{K - 1}}{z}^{k + 1/2}. $$ For proof, see Appendix A An important issue of convergence is the choice of $\tau$ . If $\tau = 0$ we have the fastest convergence rate, on the other hand, this means that we must send full ${F}_{m}$ in each iteration (because we update ${w}^{k}$ ). This is disadvantageous from a communication point of view. The next corollaries give the rules for the right choice of $\tau$ , as well as the iterative (in deterministic case), oracle (in stochastic) and communication complexities of Algorithm 1 in both cases. The method without quantization (for example, the ordinary distributed extragradient method) in one iteration transmits the number of information proportional to $\Omega \left( {bdM}\right)$ bits, then here we measure the communication complexity in in terms of $\Omega \left( {bdM}\right)$ . Corollary 1 (Convergence of MASHA1 in the deterministic case) Let the deterministic problem (3)-(4) be solved by MASHA1 with precision $\varepsilon$ . Let Assumption 1 and one of the two cases from Assumption 2 be satisfied. If we choose $$ \tau = 1 - \beta \mathrel{\text{:=}} 1 - \frac{1}{2}\left( {\frac{1}{M}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{m = 1}}^{M}{\beta }_{m}^{\text{dev }} + {\beta }^{\text{serv }}}\right) , \tag{12} $$ then we have the following estimates for the total # of iterations and the total # of transferred bits: - in the strongly-monotone/convex case: $$ \mathcal{O}\left( {\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{\beta } + \frac{{C}_{q}}{\sqrt{\beta }\left( {{\mu }_{F} + {\mu }_{h}}\right) }}\right\rbrack \log \frac{2{\begin{Vmatrix}{z}^{0} - {z}^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}^{2}}{\varepsilon }}\right) \text{iters,}\;\mathcal{O}\left( {\left\lbrack {1 + \frac{\sqrt{\beta }{C}_{q}}{{\mu }_{F} + {\mu }_{h}}}\right\rbrack \log \frac{2{\begin{Vmatrix}{z}^{0} - {z}^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}^{2}}{\varepsilon }}\right) \text{bits,} $$ - in the monotone/convex case $$ \mathcal{O}\left( \frac{{C}_{q}\mathop{\max }\limits_{{u \in \mathcal{C}}}\left\lbrack {\begin{Vmatrix}{z}^{0} - u\end{Vmatrix}}^{2}\right\rbrack }{\sqrt{\beta }\varepsilon }\right) \text{ iters,}\;\mathcal{O}\left( \frac{\sqrt{\beta }{C}_{q}\mathop{\max }\limits_{{u \in \mathcal{C}}}\left\lbrack {\begin{Vmatrix}{z}^{0} - u\end{Vmatrix}}^{2}\right\rbrack }{\varepsilon }\right) \text{bits.} $$ One can see that our Algorithm 1 can outperform the uncompressed extragradient method. Let us compare them in the monotone case. The communication complexity of the extragra-dient method is $\mathcal{O}\left( {L\mathop{\max }\limits_{{u \in \mathcal{C}}}\left\lbrack {\begin{Vmatrix}{z}^{0} - u\end{Vmatrix}}^{2}\right\rbrack {\varepsilon }^{-1}}\right)$ . Let us consider the case when ${L}_{m} = L$ for all $m \in \{ 1,2,\ldots , M\}$ and ${q}_{m}^{\text{dev }} = q$ . Then MASHA1 has communication complexity $\mathcal{O}\left( {L\mathop{\max }\limits_{{u \in \mathcal{C}}}\left\lbrack {\begin{Vmatrix}{z}^{0} - u\end{Vmatrix}}^{2}\right\rbrack {\varepsilon }^{-1}\sqrt{\beta {q}^{\operatorname{serv}\left( {1 + q/M}\right) }}}\right)$ . If $\beta {q}^{\operatorname{serv}\left( {1 + q/M}\right) } < 1$ , we outperform the standard uncompressed extragradient method. Corollary 2 (Convergence of MASHA1 in the stochastic case) Let the stochastic problem (3)-(5) be solved by MASHA1 with precision $\varepsilon$ . Let Assumption 1 and one of the two cases from Assumption 2 be satisfied. If we choose $$ \tau = 1 - \min \left( {\frac{1}{r};\beta }\right) $$ then we have the following estimates for the total # of oracle calls and the total # of transferred bits: - in the strongly-monotone/convex case: $$ \mathcal{O}\left( {\left\lbrack {\max \left( {r;\frac{1}{\beta }}\right) + \max \left( {\sqrt{r};\frac{1}{\sqrt{\beta }}}\right) \frac{{C}_{q}}{\left( {\mu }_{F} + {\mu }_{h}\right) }}\right\rbrack \log \frac{2{\begin{Vmatrix}{z}^{0} - {z}^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}^{2}}{\varepsilon }}\right. \text{calls,} $$ $$ \mathcal{O}\left( {\left\lbrack {\max \left( {1;{r\beta }}\right) + \max \left( {\sqrt{r{\beta }^{2}};\sqrt{\beta }}\right) \frac{{C}_{q}}{{\mu }_{F} + {\mu }_{h}}}\right\rbrack \log \frac{2{\begin{Vmatrix}{z}^{0} - {z}^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}^{2}}{\varepsilon }}\right) \text{bits,} $$ - in the monotone/convex case $$ \mathcal{O}\left( {\max \left( {r;\frac{1}{\beta }}\right) \frac{{C}_{q}\mathop{\max }\limits_{{u \in \mathcal{C}}}\left\lbrack {\begin{Vmatrix}{z}^{0} - u\end{Vmatrix}}^{2}\right\rbrack }{\varepsilon }}\right) \text{calls,}\mathcal{O}\left( {\max \left( {\sqrt{r{\beta }^{2}};\sqrt{\beta }}\right) \frac{{C}_{q}\mathop{\max }\limits_{{u \in \mathcal{C}}}\left\lbrack {\begin{Vmatrix}{z}^{0} - u\end{Vmatrix}}^{2}\right\rbrack }{\varepsilon }}\right) \text{bits.} $$ In the case of a finite sum, in addition to the number of transmitted information, it is not iterations are important to us, but the number of calls to the oracle for ${F}_{m, r}$ . This is due to the fact that it is $r$ times more expensive to calculate full ${F}_{m}$ , and the calculation of ${F}_{m}$ should be avoided. For deterministic case (when $r = 1$ ) estimates from Corollary 2 is the same as in Corollary 1 . ## 5 EXPERIMENTS ### 5.1 BILINEAR SADDLE POINT PROBLEM We start our experiments with a distributed bilinear problem: $$ \mathop{\min }\limits_{{x \in {\mathbb{R}}^{d}}}\mathop{\max }\limits_{{y \in {\mathbb{R}}^{d}}}f\left( {x, y}\right) \mathrel{\text{:=}} \frac{1}{M}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{m = 1}}^{M}{f}_{m}\left( {x, y}\right) ,\;{f}_{m}\left( {x, y}\right) \mathrel{\text{:=}} {x}^{\top }{A}_{m}y + {a}_{m}^{\top }x + {b}_{m}^{\top }y + \frac{\lambda }{2}\parallel x{\parallel }^{2} - \frac{\lambda }{2}\parallel y{\parallel }^{2}, $$ (13) where ${A}_{m} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{d \times d},{a}_{m},{b}_{m} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{d}$ . This problem is a saddle point, $F$ is written out for it as follows $F\left( {x, y}\right) \mathrel{\text{:=}} \left( {{\nabla }_{x}f\left( {x, y}\right) ; - {\nabla }_{y}f\left( {x, y}\right) }\right)$ . This operator is $\lambda$ strongly monotone and, moreover, all ${F}_{m}$ are $\left( {{\begin{Vmatrix}{A}_{m}\end{Vmatrix}}_{2} + \lambda }\right)$ -Lipschitz. Therefore, such a distributed problem is well suited for the primary comparison of our methods. We take $d = {100}$ and generate positive definite matrices ${A}_{m}$ and vectors ${a}_{m},{b}_{m}$ randomly. Next, we present a series of experiments that test our theoretical results and hypotheses: - The purpose of the first experiment is to understand how much the MASHA1 and MASHA2 techniques are superior to those in the literature. As a comparison, we take QGD with natural dithering Horvath et al. (2019), classic error feedback with Top 30% compression, as well as an extra step method, each step of which is used with natural rounding, in MASHA1 (Algorithm 1) we also used natural dithering, in MASHA2 (Algorithm 2) - Top30%. See results in Figure 1. Figure 1: Comparison MASHA1 (Algorithm 1) and MASHA2 (Algorithm 2) with existing methods in iterations and in Mbytes. ![01965b10-1a9e-7630-a928-7048c19904fa_7_382_1222_1030_294_0.jpg](images/01965b10-1a9e-7630-a928-7048c19904fa_7_382_1222_1030_294_0.jpg) We see that methods based on gradient descent (QSG and EF) diverge, this confirms the use of a method specific for saddles (for example, an extragradient). The much slower convergence of the quantizied extragradient method shows the efficiency of approach, when we compress the difference ${F}_{m}\left( {z}^{k + 1/2}\right) - F\left( {w}^{k}\right)$ . ### 5.2 ADVERSARIAL TRAINING OF TRANSFORMERS In this section, we evaluate how compression performs for variational inequalities (and for saddle point problems, as a special case) in a more practically motivated scenario. Indeed, saddle point problems (special case of variational inequalities) have wide applications in machine learning (see Appendix D). In particular, in adversarial training. We consider on of these tasks and train Transformer-based masked language model (Vaswani et al., 2017; Devlin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019) using a fleet of 16 low-cost preemptible workers with T4 GPU with low-bandwidth interconnect. For this task, we use the compute-efficient adversarial training regimen proposed for transformers by Zhu et al. (2019); Liu et al. (2020). Formally, the adversarial formulation of the problem is a min-max problem: $$ \mathop{\min }\limits_{w}\mathop{\max }\limits_{{\begin{Vmatrix}{\rho }_{1}\end{Vmatrix} \leq e,\ldots \begin{Vmatrix}{\rho }_{N}\end{Vmatrix} \leq e}}\frac{1}{N}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{n = 1}}^{N}l{\left( f{\left( w,{x}_{n} + {\rho }_{n},{y}_{n}\right) }^{2} + \frac{\lambda }{2}\parallel w{\parallel }^{2} - \frac{\beta }{2}\parallel \rho {\parallel }^{2}\right) }^{2}, $$ where $w$ are the weights of the model, ${\left\{ \left( {x}_{n},{y}_{n}\right) \right\} }_{n = 1}^{N}$ are pairs of the training data, $\rho$ is the so-called adversarial noise, which introduces a perturbation in the data, and $\lambda$ and $\beta$ are the regularizers. To make our setup more realistic, we train ALBERT-large with layer sharing (Lan et al., 2020), which was recently shown to be much more communication-efficient during training (Ryabinin et al., 2021; Diskin et al., 2021). We train our model on a combination of Bookcorpus and Wikipedia datasets with same optimizer (LAMB) and parameters as in the original paper (Lan et al., 2020), use the adversarial training configuration from Zhu et al. (2019) and follow system design considerations for preemptible instances (Ryabinin et al., 2021). In terms of communication, we consider 4 different setups for gradient compression: the "baseline" strategy with uncompressed gradients, full 8-bit quantization (Dettmers, 2015; Lin et al., 2018), mixed 8-bit quantization, and Power compression (Vogels et al.,2019) with rank $r = 8$ . For mixed 8-bit quantization and Power we only apply compression to gradient tensors with more than ${2}^{16}$ elements, sending smaller ones uncompressed. These small tensors represent layer biases and LayerNorm scales (Ba et al.,2016) that collectively amount to $\leq 1\%$ of the total gradient, but can be more difficult to compress that regular weight tensors. Finally, since Power is a biased compression algorithm, we use error feedback (Karimireddy et al., 2019; Richtárik et al., 2021) with modified formulation proposed by Vogels et al. (2019). For all experimental setups, we report learning curves in terms of model training objective, similarly to (Fedus et al., 2021; Ryabinin et al., 2021). To better quantify the differences in training loss, we also evaluate the downstream performance for each model on several popular tasks from (Wang et al. 2018) after each model was trained on approximately 80 billion tokens. Finally, we measure the communication efficiency of each proposed strategy by measuring the average wall time per communication round when all 16 workers are active. The learning curves on Figure 1(upper) follow a predictable pattern, with more extreme compression techniques demonstrating slower per-iteration convergence. One curious exception to that is full 8-bit quantization, which was unable to achieve competitive training loss. The remaining three setups converge to similar loss values below 2 . Both the baseline and mixed 8-bit compression show similar values in terms of downstream performance, with Power compression showing mild degradation. But in terms of information transfer time, methods using compression (especially Power) are significantly superior to the method without compression. This makes it possible to use such techniques to increase the training time without sacrificing quality. summary_of_the_paper: The authors have considered general distributed variational inequalities problems and proposed two methods using unbiased and contractive compressors.They have evaluated their methods on saddle point problems including large-scale adversarial training of transformers. 


main_review: The main weakness of this paper is regarding the theoretical results. 

- The authors consider a general notion of unbiased compression schemes in (1). Parameter $q$ is in general dimension-dependent (Alistarh 2017). The authors establish the bounds by treating $q$ as a constant term. However, this parameter can be very large in overparameterized settings, which motivate this paper as stated in the abstract. When $q$ is large, $C_q$ in Theorem 1 will be large too, which leads to very small learning rate. Similar issue happens when $\tau$ is close to one. As authors mentioned $\tau$ should be close to one to control communication costs. When $\tau$ is close to one, the learning rate becomes very small, which does not lead to interesting results in terms of convergence. A similar issue happens in Corollaries 1 and 2.

- I think the discussion after Corollary 1 is not accurate. In particular, the condition under which Algorithm 1 outperforms the standard uncompressed extragradient method is restrictive. It is more likely that the standard uncompressed extragradient method outperforms Algorithm 1 in terms of communication complexity. 

-  It will be nice if the authors provide concrete examples of interesting VI problems beyond saddle point problems in machine learning. It is also important to show that Assumptions 1 and 2 hold for such problems. Indeed, the experiments are also based on saddle point problems. 

- It is unclear how all nodes have access to $F(w^{k+1})$ at the beginning of the iteration $k+1$ while only some nodes with $b_k=1$ compute $F_m(w^{k+1})$?

- In Table 1, the authors mentioned that ``(Deng & Mahdavi 2021) does not have strong theory since it cannot improve on non-compressed methods without assuming data homogeneity.'' I my view, a similar criticism applies to this work too. 

- "we introduce the notion of expected density, defined ..." This is not new. A similar notion based on the expected number of required bits has been proposed in the literature e.g., QSGD, NUQSGD, signSGD ...

- The paper is not well-written. There are many typos that require a substantial revision. Some examples include: abstract, Section 1.4, footnotes in Table 1, first paragraph of Section 4.1, first paragraph of Section 5.2, ...

Minor comment: 
- Section 4.2: "We now establish convergence of MASHA1 in both regimes": please specify "both regimes". 

- Some terms such as $\tau$ and $b_k$ are defined only in Algorithm 1. It will be easier for readers if those terms are defined in the main text too.  
summary_of_the_review: The paper has some interesting aspects for example large-scale adversarial training of transformers. However, given the issues regarding theoretical results, connection with related work, and clarify and presentation of the paper, I recommend rejection.

# FEW-SHOT LEARNING VIA LEARNING THE REPRESENTATION, PROVABLY

Anonymous authors

Paper under double-blind review

## Abstract

This paper studies few-shot learning via representation learning, where one uses $T$ source tasks with ${n}_{1}$ data per task to learn a representation in order to reduce the sample complexity of a target task for which there is only ${n}_{2}\left( { \ll  {n}_{1}}\right)$ data. Specifically, we focus on the setting where there exists a good common representation between source and target, and our goal is to understand how much a sample size reduction is possible. First, we study the setting where this common representation is low-dimensional and provide a risk bound of $\widetilde{O}\left( {\frac{dk}{{n}_{1}T} + \frac{k}{{n}_{2}}}\right)$ on the target task for the linear representation class; here $d$ is the ambient input dimension and $k\left( { \ll  d}\right)$ is the dimension of the representation. This result bypasses the $\Omega \left( \frac{1}{T}\right)$ barrier under the i.i.d. task assumption, and can capture the desired property that all ${n}_{1}T$ samples from source tasks can be pooled together for representation learning. We further extend this result to handle a general representation function class and obtain a similar result. Next, we consider the setting where the common representation may be high-dimensional but is capacity-constrained (say in norm); here, we again demonstrate the advantage of representation learning in both high-dimensional linear regression and neural networks, and show that representation learning can fully utilize all ${n}_{1}T$ samples from source tasks.

## 1 INTRODUCTION

A popular scheme for few-shot learning, i.e., learning in a data scarce environment, is representation learning, where one first learns a feature extractor, or representation, e.g., the last layer of a convolutional neural network, from different but related source tasks, and then uses a simple predictor (usually a linear function) on top of this representation in the target task. The hope is that the learned representation captures the common structure across tasks, which makes a linear predictor sufficient for the target task. If the learned representation is good enough, it is possible that a few samples are sufficient for learning the target task, which can be much smaller than the number of samples required to learn the target task from scratch.

While representation learning has achieved tremendous success in a variety of applications (Bengio et al. 2013), its theoretical studies are limited. In existing theoretical work, the most natural algorithm is to explicitly look for the optimal representation given source data, which when combined with a (different) linear predictor on top for each task can achieve the smallest cumulative training error on the source tasks. Of course, it is not guaranteed that the representation found will be useful for the target task unless one makes some assumptions to characterize the connections between different tasks. Existing work often imposes a probabilistic assumption about the connection between tasks: each task is sampled i.i.d. from an underlying distribution. Under this assumption, Maurer et al. (2016) showed an $\widetilde{O}\left( {\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{{n}_{2}}}}\right)$ risk bound on the target task, where $T$ is the number of source tasks, ${n}_{1}$ is the number of samples per source task, and ${n}_{2}$ is the number of samples from the target task. Unsatisfactorily, this bound necessarily requires the number of tasks $T$ to be large, and it does not improve when the number of samples per source task, ${n}_{1}$ , increases. Intuitively, one should expect more data to help, and therefore an ideal bound would be $\frac{1}{\sqrt{{n}_{1}T}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{{n}_{2}}}$ (or $\frac{1}{{n}_{1}T} + \frac{1}{{n}_{2}}$ in the realizable case), because ${n}_{1}T$ is the total number of training data points from source tasks, which can be potentially pooled to learn the representation. Unfortunately, as pointed out by Maurer et al. (2016), there exists an example that satisfies the i.i.d. task assumption for which $\Omega \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}\right)$ is unavoidable (or $\Omega \left( \frac{1}{T}\right)$ in the realizable setting). This means that the i.i.d. assumption alone is not sufficient if we want to take advantage of a large amount of samples per task. Therefore, a natural question is:

---

${}^{1}$ We only focus on the dependence on $T,{n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ in this paragraph. Note that Maurer et al. (2016) only considered ${n}_{1} = {n}_{2}$ , but their approach does not give a better result even if ${n}_{1} > {n}_{2}$ .

---

What connections between tasks enable representation learning to utilize all source data?

In this paper, we obtain the first set of results that fully utilize the ${n}_{1}T$ data from source tasks. We replace the i.i.d. assumption over tasks with natural structural conditions on the input distributions and linear predictors. These conditions depict that the target task can be in some sense "covered" by the source tasks, which will further give rise to the desirable guarantees.

First, we study the setting where there exists a common well-specified low-dimensional representation in source and target tasks, and obtain an $\widetilde{O}\left( {\frac{dk}{{n}_{1}T} + \frac{k}{{n}_{2}}}\right)$ risk bound on the target task where $d$ is the ambient input dimension, $k\left( { \ll  d}\right)$ is the dimension of the representation, and ${n}_{2}$ is the number of data from the target task. Note that this improves the $\frac{d}{{n}_{2}}$ rate of just learning the target task without using representation learning. The term $\frac{dk}{{n}_{1}T}$ indicates that we can fully exploit all ${n}_{1}T$ data in the source tasks to learn the representation. We further extend this result to handle general representation function class and obtain an $\widetilde{O}\left( {\frac{\mathcal{C}\left( \Phi \right) }{{n}_{1}T} + \frac{k}{{n}_{2}}}\right)$ risk bound on the target task, where $\Phi$ is the representation function class and $\mathcal{C}\left( \Phi \right)$ is a certain complexity measure of $\Phi$ .

Second, we study the setting where there exists a common linear high-dimensional representation for source and target tasks, and obtain an $\widetilde{O}\left( {\frac{\bar{R}\sqrt{\operatorname{Tr}\left( \sum \right) }}{\sqrt{{n}_{1}T}} + \frac{\bar{R}\sqrt{\parallel \sum {\parallel }_{2}}}{\sqrt{{n}_{2}}}}\right)$ rate where $\bar{R}$ is a normalized nuclear norm control over linear predictors, and $\sum$ is the covariance matrix of the raw feature. This also improves over the baseline rate for the case without using representation learning. We further extend this result to two-layer neural networks with ReLU activation. Again, our results indicate that we can fully exploit ${n}_{1}T$ source data.

A technical insight coming out of our analysis is that any capacity controlled method that gets low test error on the source tasks must also get low test error on the target task by virtue of being forced to learn a good representation. Our result on high-dimensional representations shows that the capacity control for representation learning does not have to be through explicit low dimensionality.

Organization. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. We review related work in Section 2. In Section 3, we formally describe the setting we consider. In Section 4, we present our main result for low-dimensional linear representation learning. A generalization to nonlinear representation classes is deferred to Appendix B. In Section 5, we present our main result for high-dimensional linear representation learning. In Section 6, we present our result for representation learning in neural networks. We conclude in Section 7 and leave most of the proofs to appendices.

## 2 RELATED WORK

The idea of multitask representation learning at least dates back to Caruana (1997); Thrun and Pratt (1998); Baxter (2000). Empirically, representation learning has shown its great power in various domains; see Bengio et al. (2013) for a survey. In particular, representation learning is widely adopted for few-shot learning tasks (Sun et al., 2017; Goyal et al., 2019). Representation learning is also closely connected to meta-learning (Schaul and Schmidhuber, 2010). Recent work Raghu et al. (2019) empirically suggested that the effectiveness of the popular meta-learning algorithm Model Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) is due to its ability to learn a useful representation. The scheme we analyze in this paper is closely related to Lee et al. (2019); Bertinetto et al. (2018) for meta-learning.

On the theoretical side, Baxter (2000) performed the first theoretical analysis and gave sample complexity bounds using covering numbers. Maurer et al. (2016) and follow-up work gave analyses on the benefit of representation learning for reducing the sample complexity of the target task. They assumed every task is i.i.d. drawn from an underlying distribution and can obtain an $\widetilde{O}\left( {\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{{n}_{2}}}}\right)$ rate. As pointed out in Maurer et al. (2016), the $\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}$ dependence is not improvable even if ${n}_{1} \rightarrow  \infty$ because $\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}$ is the rate of concentration for the distribution over tasks. The concurrent work of Tripuraneni et al. (2020) studies low-dimensional linear representation learning and obtains a similar result as ours in this case, but they assume isotropic inputs for all tasks, which is a special case of our result. Furthermore we also provide results for high-dimensional linear representations, general non-linear representations, and two-layer neural networks. Tripuraneni et al. (2020) also give a computationally efficient algorithm for standard Gaussian inputs and a lower bound for subspace recovery in the low-dimensional linear setting.

Another recent line of theoretical work analyzed gradient-based meta-learning methods (Denevi et al. 2019; Finn et al., 2019; Khodak et al., 2019) and showed guarantees for convex losses by using tools from online convex optimization. Lastly, we remark that there are analyses for other representation learning schemes (Arora et al., 2019; McNamara and Balcan, 2017; Galanti et al., 2016; Alquier et al., 2016; Denevi et al., 2018).

## 3 NOTATION AND SETUP

Notation. Let $\left\lbrack  n\right\rbrack   = \{ 1,2,\ldots , n\}$ . We use $\parallel  \cdot  \parallel$ or $\parallel  \cdot  {\parallel }_{2}$ to denote the ${\ell }_{2}$ norm of a vector or the spectral norm of a matrix. Denote by $\parallel  \cdot  {\parallel }_{F}$ and $\parallel  \cdot  {\parallel }_{ * }$ the Frobenius norm and the nuclear norm of a matrix, respectively. Let $\langle  \cdot  , \cdot  \rangle$ be the Euclidean inner product between vectors or matrices. Denote by $I$ the identity matrix. Let $\mathcal{N}\left( {\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}}\right) /\mathcal{N}\left( {\mathbf{\mu },\sum }\right)$ be the one-dimensional/multi-dimensional Gaussian distribution, and ${\chi }^{2}\left( m\right)$ the chi-squared distribution with $m$ degrees of freedom.

For a matrix $A \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{m \times  n}$ , let ${\sigma }_{i}\left( A\right)$ be its $i$ -th largest singular value. Let $\operatorname{span}\left( A\right)$ be the subspace of ${\mathbb{R}}^{m}$ spanned by the columns of $A$ , i.e., span $\left( A\right)  = \left\{  {A\mathbf{v} \mid  \mathbf{v} \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{n}}\right\}$ . Denote ${P}_{A} = A{\left( {A}^{\top }A\right) }^{ \dagger  }{A}^{\top } \in$ ${\mathbb{R}}^{m \times  m}$ , which is the projection matrix onto span(A). Here ${}^{ \dagger  }$ stands for the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse. Note that $0 \preccurlyeq  {P}_{A} \preccurlyeq  I$ and ${P}_{A}^{2} = {P}_{A}$ . We also define ${P}_{A}^{ \bot  } = I - {P}_{A}$ , which is the projection matrix onto $\operatorname{span}{\left( A\right) }^{ \bot  }$ , the orthogonal complement of $\operatorname{span}\left( A\right)$ in ${\mathbb{R}}^{m}$ . For a positive semidefinite (psd) matrix $B$ , denote by ${\lambda }_{\max }\left( B\right)$ and ${\lambda }_{\min }\left( B\right)$ its largest and smallest eigenvalues, respectively; let ${B}^{1/2}$ be the psd matrix such that ${\left( {B}^{1/2}\right) }^{2} = B$ .

We use the standard $O\left( \cdot \right) ,\Omega \left( \cdot \right)$ and $\Theta \left( \cdot \right)$ notation to hide universal constant factors. We also use $a \lesssim  b$ or $b \gtrsim  a$ to indicate $a = O\left( b\right)$ , and use $a \gg  b$ or $b \ll  a$ to mean that $a \geq  C \cdot  b$ for a sufficiently large universal constant $C > 0$ .

### 3.1 Problem Setup

Suppose that there are $T$ source tasks. Each task $t \in  \left\lbrack  T\right\rbrack$ is associated with a distribution ${\mu }_{t}$ over the joint data space $\mathrm{X} \times  \mathrm{Y}$ , where $\mathrm{X}$ is the input space and $\mathrm{Y}$ is the output space. In this paper we consider $\mathsf{X} \subseteq  {\mathbb{R}}^{d}$ and $\mathsf{Y} \subseteq  \mathbb{R}$ . For each source task $t \in  \left\lbrack  T\right\rbrack$ we have access to ${n}_{1}$ i.i.d. samples $\left( {{\mathbf{x}}_{t,1},{y}_{t,1}}\right) ,\ldots ,\left( {{\mathbf{x}}_{t,{n}_{1}},{y}_{t,{n}_{1}}}\right)$ from ${\mu }_{t}$ . For convenience, we express these ${n}_{1}$ samples collectively as an input matrix ${X}_{t} \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{{n}_{1} \times  d}$ and an output vector ${\mathbf{y}}_{t} \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{{n}_{1}}$ .

Multitask learning tries to learn prediction functions for all the $T$ source tasks simultaneously in the hope of discovering some underlying common property of these tasks. The common property we consider in this paper is a representation, which is a function $\phi  : \mathrm{X} \rightarrow  \mathrm{Z}$ that maps an input to some feature space $\mathrm{Z} \subseteq  {\mathbb{R}}^{k}$ . We restrict the representation function to be in some function class $\Phi$ , e.g., neural networks. We try to use different linear predictors on top of a common representation function $\phi$ to model the input-output relations in different source tasks. Namely, for each task $t \in  \left\lbrack  T\right\rbrack$ , we set the prediction function to be $\mathbf{x} \mapsto  \left\langle  {{\mathbf{w}}_{t},\phi \left( \mathbf{x}\right) }\right\rangle  \left( {{\mathbf{w}}_{t} \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{k}}\right)$ . Therefore, using the training samples from $T$ tasks, we can solve the following optimization problem to learn the representation:2

$$
\mathop{\operatorname{minimize}}\limits_{{\phi  \in  \Phi ,{\mathbf{w}}_{1},\ldots ,{\mathbf{w}}_{T} \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{k}}}\frac{1}{2{n}_{1}T}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{t = 1}}^{T}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{{n}_{1}}{\left( {y}_{t, i} - \left\langle  {\mathbf{w}}_{t},\phi \left( {\mathbf{x}}_{t, i}\right) \right\rangle  \right) }^{2}. \tag{1}
$$

We overload the notation to allow $\phi$ to apply to all the samples in a data matrix simultaneously, i.e., $\phi \left( {X}_{t}\right)  = {\left\lbrack  \phi \left( {\mathbf{x}}_{t,1}\right) ,\ldots ,\phi \left( {\mathbf{x}}_{t,{n}_{1}}\right) \right\rbrack  }^{\top } \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{{n}_{1} \times  k}$ . Then (1) can be rewritten as

$$
\mathop{\operatorname{minimize}}\limits_{{\phi  \in  \Phi ,{\mathbf{w}}_{1},\ldots ,{\mathbf{w}}_{T} \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{k}}}\frac{1}{2{n}_{1}T}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{t = 1}}^{T}{\begin{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{y}}_{t} - \phi \left( {X}_{t}\right) {\mathbf{w}}_{t}\end{Vmatrix}}^{2}. \tag{2}
$$

---

${}^{2}$ We use the ${\ell }_{2}$ loss throughout this paper.

---

Let $\widehat{\phi } \in  \Phi$ be the representation function obtained by solving (2). Now we retain this representation and apply it to future (target) tasks. For a target task specified by a distribution ${\mu }_{T + 1}$ over $\mathrm{X} \times  \mathrm{Y}$ , suppose we receive ${n}_{2}$ i.i.d. samples ${X}_{T + 1} \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{{n}_{2} \times  d},{\mathbf{y}}_{T + 1} \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{{n}_{2}}$ . We further train a linear predictor on top of $\widehat{\phi }$ for this task:

$$
\mathop{\operatorname{minimize}}\limits_{{{\mathbf{w}}_{T + 1} \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{k}}}\frac{1}{2{n}_{2}}{\begin{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{y}}_{T + 1} - \widehat{\phi }\left( {X}_{T + 1}\right) {\mathbf{w}}_{T + 1}\end{Vmatrix}}^{2}. \tag{3}
$$

Let ${\widehat{w}}_{T + 1}$ be the returned solution. We are interested in whether our learned predictor $x \mapsto$ $\left\langle  {{\widehat{\mathbf{w}}}_{T + 1},\widehat{\phi }\left( \mathbf{x}\right) }\right\rangle$ works well on average for the target task, i.e., we want the population loss

$$
{L}_{{\mu }_{T + 1}}\left( {\widehat{\phi },{\widehat{\mathbf{w}}}_{T + 1}}\right)  = {\mathbb{E}}_{\left( {\mathbf{x}, y}\right)  \sim  {\mu }_{T + 1}}\frac{1}{2}{\left( y-\langle {\widehat{\mathbf{w}}}_{T + 1},\widehat{\phi }\left( \mathbf{x}\right) \rangle \right) }^{2}
$$

to be small. In particular, we are interested in the few-shot learning setting, where the number of samples ${n}_{2}$ from the target task is small - much smaller than the number of samples required for learning the target task from scratch.

Data assumption. In order for the above learning procedure to make sense, we assume that there is a ground-truth optimal representation function ${\phi }^{ * } \in  \Phi$ and specializations ${\mathbf{w}}_{1}^{ * },\ldots ,{\mathbf{w}}_{T + 1}^{ * } \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{k}$ for all the tasks such that for each task $t \in  \left\lbrack  {T + 1}\right\rbrack$ , we have ${\mathbb{E}}_{\left( {\mathbf{x}, y}\right)  \sim  {\mu }_{t}}\left\lbrack  {y \mid  \mathbf{x}}\right\rbrack   = \left\langle  {{\mathbf{w}}_{t}^{ * },{\phi }^{ * }\left( \mathbf{x}\right) }\right\rangle$ . More specifically, we assume $\left( {\mathbf{x}, y}\right)  \sim  {\mu }_{t}$ can be generated by

$$
y = \left\langle  {{\mathbf{w}}_{t}^{ * },{\phi }^{ * }\left( \mathbf{x}\right) }\right\rangle   + z,\;\mathbf{x} \sim  {p}_{t}, z \sim  \mathcal{N}\left( {0,{\sigma }^{2}}\right) , \tag{4}
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ and $z$ are independent. Our goal is to bound the excess risk of our learned model on the target task, i.e., how much our learned model $\left( {\widehat{\phi },{\widehat{w}}_{T + 1}}\right)$ performs worse than the optimal model $\left( {{\phi }^{ * },{\mathbf{w}}_{T + 1}^{ * }}\right)$ on the target task:

$$
\operatorname{ER}\left( {\widehat{\phi },{\widehat{\mathbf{w}}}_{T + 1}}\right)  = {L}_{{\mu }_{T + 1}}\left( {\widehat{\phi },{\widehat{\mathbf{w}}}_{T + 1}}\right)  - {L}_{{\mu }_{T + 1}}\left( {{\phi }^{ * },{\mathbf{w}}_{T + 1}^{ * }}\right)
$$

$$
= \frac{1}{2}{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{x} \sim  {p}_{T + 1}}\left\lbrack  {\left( \left\langle  {\widehat{\mathbf{w}}}_{T + 1},\widehat{\phi }\left( \mathbf{x}\right) \right\rangle   - \left\langle  {\mathbf{w}}_{T + 1}^{ * },{\phi }^{ * }\left( \mathbf{x}\right) \right\rangle  \right) }^{2}\right\rbrack  . \tag{5}
$$

Here we have used the relation (4). Oftentimes we are interested in the average performance on a random target task (i.e., ${\mathbf{w}}_{T + 1}^{ * }$ is random). In such case we look at the expected excess risk ${\mathbb{E}}_{{\mathbf{w}}_{T + 1}^{ * }}\left\lbrack  {\operatorname{ER}\left( {\widehat{\phi },{\widehat{\mathbf{w}}}_{T + 1}}\right) }\right\rbrack$ .

## 4 Low-Dimensional Linear Representations

In this section, we consider the case where the representation is a linear map from the original input space ${\mathbb{R}}^{d}$ to a low-dimensional space ${\mathbb{R}}^{k}\left( {k \ll  d}\right)$ . Namely, we let the representation function class be $\Phi  = \left\{  {\mathbf{x} \mapsto  {B}^{\top }\mathbf{x} \mid  B \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{d \times  k}}\right\}$ . Then the optimization problem (2) for learning the representation can be written as

$$
\left( {\widehat{B},\widehat{W}}\right)  \leftarrow  \underset{\begin{matrix} {B \in  \mathbb{R}k : k} \\  {W = \left\lbrack  {{w}_{1},\ldots ,{w}_{T}}\right\rbrack   \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{k \times  T}} \end{matrix}}{\arg \min }\frac{1}{2{n}_{1}T}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{t = 1}}^{T}{\begin{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{y}}_{t} - {X}_{t}B{\mathbf{w}}_{t}\end{Vmatrix}}^{2}. \tag{6}
$$

The inputs from $T$ source tasks, ${X}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{T} \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{{n}_{1} \times  d}$ , can be written in the form of a linear operator $\mathcal{X} : {\mathbb{R}}^{d \times  T} \rightarrow  {\mathbb{R}}^{{n}_{1} \times  T}$ , where

$$
\mathcal{X}\left( \Theta \right)  = \left\lbrack  {{X}_{1}{\mathbf{\theta }}_{1},\ldots ,{X}_{T}{\mathbf{\theta }}_{T}}\right\rbrack  ,\;\forall \Theta  = \left\lbrack  {{\mathbf{\theta }}_{1},\ldots ,{\mathbf{\theta }}_{T}}\right\rbrack   \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{d \times  T}.
$$

With this notation, (6) can be rewritten as

$$
\left( {\widehat{B},\widehat{W}}\right)  \leftarrow  \underset{B \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{d \times  k}, W \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{k \times  T}}{\arg \min }\frac{1}{2{n}_{1}T}\parallel Y - \mathcal{X}\left( {BW}\right) {\parallel }_{F}^{2}, \tag{7}
$$

where $Y = \left\lbrack  {{\mathbf{y}}_{1},\ldots ,{\mathbf{y}}_{T}}\right\rbrack   \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{{n}_{1} \times  T}$ .

With the learned representation $\widehat{B}$ from (7), for the target task, we further find a linear function on top of the representation:

$$
{\widehat{\mathbf{w}}}_{T + 1} \leftarrow  \underset{\mathbf{w} \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{k}}{\arg \min }\frac{1}{2{n}_{2}}{\begin{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{y}}_{T + 1} - {X}_{T + 1}\widehat{B}\mathbf{w}\end{Vmatrix}}^{2}. \tag{8}
$$

As described in Section 3, we assume that all $T + 1$ tasks share a common ground-truth representation specified by a matrix ${\bar{B}}^{ * } \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{d \times  k}$ such that a sample $\left( {\mathbf{x}, y}\right)  \sim  {\mu }_{t}$ satisfies $\mathbf{x} \sim  {p}_{t}$ and $y =$ ${\left( {\mathbf{w}}_{t}^{ * }\right) }^{\top }{\left( {B}^{ * }\right) }^{\top }\mathbf{x} + z$ where $z \sim  \mathcal{N}\left( {0,{\sigma }^{2}}\right)$ is independent of $\mathbf{x}$ . Here ${\mathbf{w}}_{t}^{ * } \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{k}$ , and we assume $\begin{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{w}}_{t}^{ * }\end{Vmatrix} = \Theta \left( 1\right)$ for all $t \in  \left\lbrack  {T + 1}\right\rbrack$ . Denote ${W}^{ * } = \left\lbrack  {{\mathbf{w}}_{1}^{ * },\ldots ,{\mathbf{w}}_{T}^{ * }}\right\rbrack   \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{k \times  T}$ . Then we can write $Y = \mathcal{X}\left( {{B}^{ * }{W}^{ * }}\right)  + Z$ , where the noise matrix $Z$ has i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}\left( {0,{\sigma }^{2}}\right)$ entries.

Assume ${\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{x} \sim  {p}_{t}}\left\lbrack  \mathbf{x}\right\rbrack   = \mathbf{0}$ and let ${\sum }_{t} = {\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{x} \sim  {p}_{t}}\left\lbrack  {\mathbf{x}{\mathbf{x}}^{\top }}\right\rbrack$ for all $t \in  \left\lbrack  {T + 1}\right\rbrack$ . Note that a sample $\mathbf{x} \sim  {p}_{t}$ can be generated from $\mathbf{x} = {\sum }_{t}^{1/2}\overline{\mathbf{x}}$ for $\overline{\mathbf{x}} \sim  {\bar{p}}_{t}$ such that ${\mathbb{E}}_{\overline{\mathbf{x}} \sim  {\bar{p}}_{t}}\left\lbrack  \overline{\mathbf{x}}\right\rbrack   = \mathbf{0}$ and ${\mathbb{E}}_{\overline{\mathbf{x}} \sim  {\bar{p}}_{t}}\left\lbrack  {\overline{\mathbf{x}}{\overline{\mathbf{x}}}^{\top }}\right\rbrack   = I$ . $\left( {\bar{p}}_{t}\right.$ is called the whitening of $\left. {p}_{t}\right)$ . In this section we make the following assumptions on the input distributions ${p}_{1},\ldots ,{p}_{T + 1}$ .

Assumption 4.1 (subgaussian input). There exists $\rho  > 0$ such that, for all $t \in  \left\lbrack  {T + 1}\right\rbrack$ , the random vector $\overline{\mathbf{x}} \sim  {\bar{p}}_{t}$ is ${\rho }^{2}$ -subgaussian. ${}^{3}$

Assumption 4.2 (covariance dominance). There exists $c > 0$ such that ${\sum }_{t} \succcurlyeq  c \cdot  {\sum }_{T + 1}$ for all $t \in  \left\lbrack  T\right\rbrack$ .

Assumption 4.1 is a standard assumption in statistical learning to obtain probabilistic tail bounds used in our proof. It may be replaced with other moment or boundedness conditions if we adopt different tail bounds in the analysis.

Assumption 4.2 says that every direction spanned by ${\sum }_{T + 1}$ should also be spanned by ${\sum }_{t}\left( {t \in  \left\lbrack  T\right\rbrack  }\right)$ , and the parameter $c$ quantifies how "easy" it is for ${\sum }_{t}$ to cover ${\sum }_{T + 1}$ . Intuitively, the larger $c$ is, the easier it is to cover the target domain using source domains, and we will indeed see that the risk will be proportional to $\frac{1}{c}$ . We remark that we do not necessarily need ${\sum }_{t} \succcurlyeq  c \cdot  {\sum }_{T + 1}$ for all $t \in  \left\lbrack  T\right\rbrack$ ; as long as this holds for a constant fraction of $t$ ’s, our result is valid.

We also make the following assumption that characterizes the diversity of the source tasks.

Assumption 4.3 (diverse source tasks). The matrix ${W}^{ * } = \left\lbrack  {{w}_{1}^{ * },\ldots ,{w}_{T}^{ * }}\right\rbrack   \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{k \times  T}$ satisfies ${\sigma }_{k}^{2}\left( {W}^{ * }\right)  \geq  \Omega \left( \frac{T}{k}\right)$ .

Recall that $\begin{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{w}}_{t}^{ * }\end{Vmatrix} = \Theta \left( 1\right)$ , which implies $\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{k}{\sigma }_{j}^{2}\left( {W}^{ * }\right)  = {\begin{Vmatrix}{W}^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}_{F}^{2} = \Theta \left( T\right)$ . Thus, Assumption 4.3 is equivalent to saying that $\frac{{\sigma }_{1}\left( {W}^{ * }\right) }{{\sigma }_{k}\left( {W}^{ * }\right) } = O\left( 1\right)$ . Roughly speaking, this means that ${\left\{  {\mathbf{w}}_{t}^{ * }\right\}  }_{t \in  \left\lbrack  T\right\rbrack  }$ can cover all directions in ${\mathbb{R}}^{k}$ . As an example, Assumption 4.3 is satisfied with high probability when ${\mathbf{w}}_{t}^{ * }$ ’s are sampled i.i.d. from $\mathcal{N}\left( {0,\sum }\right)$ with $\frac{{\lambda }_{\max }\left( \sum \right) }{{\lambda }_{\min }\left( \sum \right) } = O\left( 1\right)$ .

Finally, we make the following assumption on the distribution of the target task.

Assumption 4.4 (distribution of target task). Assume that ${\mathbf{w}}_{T + 1}^{ * }$ follows a distribution $\nu$ such that $\begin{Vmatrix}{{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{w} \sim  \nu }\left\lbrack  {\mathbf{w}{\mathbf{w}}^{\top }}\right\rbrack  }\end{Vmatrix} \leq  O\left( \frac{1}{k}\right) .$

Since we assume $\begin{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{w}}_{T + 1}^{ * }\end{Vmatrix} = \Theta \left( 1\right)$ , the assumption $\begin{Vmatrix}{{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{w} \sim  \nu }\left\lbrack  {\mathbf{w}{\mathbf{w}}^{\top }}\right\rbrack  }\end{Vmatrix} \leq  O\left( \frac{1}{k}\right)$ means that the distribution of ${\mathbf{w}}_{T + 1}^{ * }$ does not align with any direction significantly more than average. It is useful to think of the uniform distribution on the unit sphere as an example, though we can allow a much more general class of distributions. This is also compatible with Assumption 4.3 which says that ${\mathbf{w}}_{t}^{ * }$ ’s cover all the directions.

Assumption 4.4 can be removed at the cost of a slightly worse risk bound. See Remark 4.1.

Our main result in this section is the following theorem.

Theorem 4.1 (main theorem for linear representations). Fix a failure probability $\delta  \in  \left( {0,1}\right)$ . Under Assumptions 4.1 4.2 4.3 and 4.4 we further assume ${2k} \leq  \min \{ d, T\}$ and that the sample sizes in source and target tasks satisfy ${n}_{1} \gg  {\rho }^{4}\left( {d + \log \frac{T}{\delta }}\right) ,{n}_{2} \gg  {\rho }^{4}\left( {k + \log \frac{1}{\delta }}\right)$ , and $c{n}_{1} \geq  {n}_{2}$ . Define $\kappa  = \frac{\mathop{\max }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  T\right\rbrack  }}{\lambda }_{\max }\left( {\sum }_{t}\right) }{\mathop{\min }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  T\right\rbrack  }}{\lambda }_{\min }\left( {\sum }_{t}\right) }$ . Then with probability at least $1 - \delta$ over the samples, the expected excess risk of the learned predictor $\mathbf{x} \mapsto  {\widehat{\mathbf{w}}}_{T + 1}^{\top }\widehat{B}\mathbf{x}$ on the target task satisfies

$$
{\mathbb{E}}_{{\mathbf{w}}_{T + 1}^{ * } \sim  \nu }\left\lbrack  {\operatorname{ER}\left( {\widehat{B},{\widehat{\mathbf{w}}}_{T + 1}}\right) }\right\rbrack   \lesssim  {\sigma }^{2}\left( {\frac{{kd}\log \left( {\kappa {n}_{1}}\right) }{c{n}_{1}T} + \frac{k + \log \frac{1}{\delta }}{{n}_{2}}}\right) . \tag{9}
$$

The proof of Theorem 4.1 is in Appendix A. Theorem 4.1 shows that it is possible to learn the target task using only $O\left( k\right)$ samples via learning a good representation from the source tasks, which is better than the baseline $O\left( d\right)$ sample complexity for linear regression, thus demonstrating the benefit of representation learning. It also shows that all ${n}_{1}T$ samples from source tasks can be pooled together, bypassing the $\Omega \left( \frac{1}{T}\right)$ barrier under the i.i.d. tasks assumption.

Remark 4.1 (deterministic target task). We can drop Assumption 4.4 and easily obtain the following excess risk bound for any deterministic ${\mathbf{w}}_{T + 1}^{ * }$ by slightly modifying the proof of Theorem 4.1:

$$
\operatorname{ER}\left( {\widehat{B},{\widehat{\mathbf{w}}}_{T + 1}}\right)  \lesssim  {\sigma }^{2}\left( {\frac{{k}^{2}d\log \left( {\kappa {n}_{1}}\right) }{c{n}_{1}T} + \frac{{k}^{2}}{c{n}_{1}} + \frac{k + \log \frac{1}{\delta }}{{n}_{2}}}\right) ,
$$

which is only at most $k$ times larger than the bound in (9).

Remark 4.2 (generalization to general nonlinear representations). Notice that low-dimensional linear representations can be described by ${kd}$ parameters. Therefore the bound in (9) has the form $\frac{\mathcal{C}\left( \Phi \right) }{{n}_{1}T} + \frac{k}{{n}_{2}}$ (ignoring logarithmic factors) where $\mathcal{C}\left( \Phi \right)$ is the complexity of $\Phi$ from parameter counting. In Appendix B, we show that it is possible to get this type of rate when $\Phi$ is a general nonlinear representation function class.

## 5 HIGH-DIMENSIONAL LINEAR REPRESENTATIONS

In this section, we consider the case where the representation is a general linear map without an explicit dimensionality constraint, and we will prove a norm-based result by exploiting the intrinsic dimension of the representation. Such a generalization is desirable since in many applications the representation dimension is not restricted.

Without loss of generality, we let the representation function class be $\Phi  = \left\{  {\mathbf{x} \mapsto  {B}^{\top }\mathbf{x} \mid  B \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{d \times  T}}\right\}$ . We note that a dimension- $T$ representation is sufficient for learning $T$ source tasks and any choice of dimension greater than $T$ will not change our argument. We use the same notation from Section 4 unless otherwise specified.

In this section we additionally assume that all tasks have the same input covariance:

Assumption 5.1. The input distributions in all tasks satisfy ${\sum }_{1} = \cdots  = {\sum }_{T + 1} = \sum$ .

Note that each task $t$ still has its own specialization function ${\mathbf{w}}_{t}^{ * }$ (c.f. [4]). We remark that there are many interesting and nontrivial scenarios under Assumption 5.1 - for example, consider the case where the inputs in each task are all images from ImageNet and each task ask asks whether the image is from a specific class.

As we will see below, we need ${\ell }_{2}$ regularization in this section, and Assumption 5.1 makes it easier to set the regularization coefficient. Nevertheless we believe Assumption 5.1 can be relaxed and leave it to future work.

Since we do not have a dimensionality constraint, we modify (7) by adding ${\ell }_{2}$ regularization:

$$
\left( {{\widehat{B}}^{\lambda },{\widehat{W}}^{\lambda }}\right)  \leftarrow  \underset{B \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{d \times  T}, W \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{T \times  T}}{\arg \min }\frac{1}{2{n}_{1}}\parallel Y - \mathcal{X}\left( {BW}\right) {\parallel }_{F}^{2} + \frac{\lambda }{2}\parallel B{\parallel }_{F}^{2} + \frac{\lambda }{2}\parallel W{\parallel }_{F}^{2}. \tag{10}
$$

For the target task, we also modify (8) by adding a norm constraint:

$$
{\widehat{\mathbf{w}}}_{T + 1}^{\lambda } \leftarrow  \underset{\parallel \mathbf{w}\parallel  \leq  r}{\arg \min }\frac{1}{2{n}_{2}}{\begin{Vmatrix}{X}_{T + 1}{\widehat{B}}^{\lambda }\mathbf{w} - {\mathbf{y}}_{T + 1}\end{Vmatrix}}^{2}. \tag{11}
$$

We will specify the choices of $\lambda$ and $r$ in Theorem 5.1.

Similar to Section 4, the source task data relation is denoted as $Y = \mathcal{X}\left( {\Theta }^{ * }\right)  + Z$ , where ${\Theta }^{ * } \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{d \times  T}$ is the ground truth and $Z$ has i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}\left( {0,{\sigma }^{2}}\right)$ entries. Suppose that the target task data satisfy ${\mathbf{y}}_{T + 1} = {X}_{T + 1}{\mathbf{\theta }}_{T + 1}^{ * } + {\mathbf{z}}_{T + 1} \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{{n}_{2}}$ . Similar to the setting in Section 4, we assume the target task data is subgaussian as in Assumption 4.1.

---

${}^{5}$ Of course, an ${\ell }_{2}$ norm constraint is also equivalent to ${\ell }_{2}$ regularization. We choose to use the constrained form here for ease of presentation.

---

Theorem 5.1 (main theorem for high-dimensional representations). Fix a failure probability $\delta  \in$ (0,1). Under Assumptions 4.1 and 5.1, we further assume ${n}_{1} \gg  {\sigma }^{2}{\rho }^{4}{\bar{R}}^{2}T \cdot  \operatorname{Tr}\left( \sum \right) \log \left( {1/\delta }\right) ,{n}_{2} \gg$ ${\sigma }^{2}{\rho }^{4}{\bar{R}}^{2}\parallel \sum \parallel \log \left( {1/\delta }\right)$ and $\overline{{n}_{1}} \geq  \overline{{n}_{2}}$ , where $\bar{R} = \parallel \Theta {\parallel }_{ * }/\sqrt{T}$ . Let the target task model ${\theta }_{T + 1}^{ * }$ be coherent with the source task models ${\Theta }^{ * }$ in the sense that ${\mathbf{\theta }}_{T + 1}^{ * } \sim  \nu  = \mathcal{N}\left( {\mathbf{0},{\Theta }^{ * }{\left( {\Theta }^{ * }\right) }^{\top }/T}\right)$ . Set $r = 2\sqrt{{\begin{Vmatrix}{\Theta }^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}_{ * }/T}$ and $\lambda  = \Theta \left( {\frac{1}{\sqrt{{n}_{1}}}{\left( \log 1/\delta \right) }^{2/3} \cdot  \left( {\sqrt{T\parallel \sum {\parallel }_{2}} + \sqrt{\operatorname{Tr}\left( \sum \right) }}\right) \log \left( {n + T}\right) }\right)$ . Then with probability at least $1 - \delta$ over the samples, the expected excess risk of the learned predictor $\mathbf{x} \mapsto  {\left( {\widehat{\mathbf{w}}}_{T + 1}^{\lambda }\right) }^{\top }{\left( {\widehat{B}}^{\lambda }\right) }^{\top }\mathbf{x}$ on the target task satisfies:

$$
{\mathbb{E}}_{{\mathbf{\theta }}_{T + 1}^{ * } \sim  \nu }\left\lbrack  {\operatorname{ER}\left( {\widehat{B},{\widehat{\mathbf{w}}}_{T + 1}}\right) }\right\rbrack   \leq  \sigma \bar{R} \cdot  \widetilde{O}\left( {\frac{\sqrt{\operatorname{Tr}\left( \sum \right) }}{\sqrt{{n}_{1}T}} + \frac{\sqrt{\parallel \sum {\parallel }_{2}}}{\sqrt{{n}_{2}}}}\right) . \tag{12}
$$

Here $\widetilde{O}$ hides logarithmic factors.

The proof of Theorem 5.1 is given in Appendix C. Note that ${\begin{Vmatrix}{\Theta }^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}_{F} = \sqrt{T}$ when each ${\mathbf{\theta }}_{t}^{ * }$ is of unit norm. Thus $\bar{R} = {\begin{Vmatrix}{\Theta }^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}_{ * }/\sqrt{T}$ should generally be regarded as $O\left( 1\right)$ for a well-behaved ${\Theta }^{ * }$ that is nearly low-dimensional. In this regime, Theorem 5.1 indicates that we are able to exploit all ${n}_{1}T$ samples from the source tasks, similar to Theorem 4.1.

With a good representation, the sample complexity on the target task can also improve over learning the target task from scratch. Consider the baseline of regular ridge regression directly applied to the target task data:

$$
{\widehat{\mathbf{\theta }}}^{\lambda } \leftarrow  \underset{\mathbf{\theta }}{\arg \min }\frac{1}{2{n}_{2}}{\begin{Vmatrix}{X}_{T + 1}\mathbf{\theta } - {\mathbf{y}}_{T + 1}\end{Vmatrix}}^{2} + \frac{\lambda }{2}\parallel \mathbf{\theta }{\parallel }^{2}. \tag{13}
$$

Its standard excess risk bound is $\operatorname{ER}\left( {\widehat{\mathbf{\theta }}}^{\lambda }\right)  \lesssim  \sigma \sqrt{\frac{{\begin{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{\theta }}_{T + 1}^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}_{2}^{2}\operatorname{Tr}\left( \sum \right) }{{n}_{2}}}$ . (See e.g. Hsu et al. (2012b).) Taking expectation over ${\mathbf{\theta }}_{T + 1}^{ * } \sim  \nu  = \mathcal{N}\left( {\mathbf{0},{\Theta }^{ * }{\left( {\Theta }^{ * }\right) }^{\top }/T}\right)$ , we obtain

$$
{\mathbb{E}}_{{\mathbf{\theta }}_{T + 1}^{ * } \sim  \nu }\left\lbrack  {\operatorname{ER}\left( {\widehat{\mathbf{\theta }}}^{\lambda }\right) }\right\rbrack   \lesssim  \sigma \frac{{\begin{Vmatrix}{\Theta }^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}_{F}}{\sqrt{T}}\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Tr}\left( \sum \right) }{{n}_{2}}}. \tag{14}
$$

Compared with (14), our bound (12) is an improvement as long as $\frac{{\begin{Vmatrix}{\Theta }^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}_{e}^{2}}{{\begin{Vmatrix}{\Theta }^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}_{F}^{2}} \ll  \frac{\operatorname{Tr}\left( \sum \right) }{\parallel \sum \parallel }$ . The left hand side $\frac{{\begin{Vmatrix}{\Theta }^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}_{\varepsilon }^{2}}{{\begin{Vmatrix}{\Theta }^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}_{P}^{2}}$ is always no more than the rank of ${\Theta }^{ * }$ , and we call it the intrinsic rank. Hence we see that we can gain from representation learning if the source predictors are intrinsically low dimensional.

To intuitively understand how this is achieved, we note that a representation $B$ is reweighing linear combinations of the features according to their "importance" on the $T$ source tasks. We make an analogy with a simple case of feature selection. Suppose we have learned a representation vector $\mathbf{b}$ where ${b}_{i}$ scales with the importance of the $i$ -th feature, i.e., the representation is $\phi \left( \mathbf{x}\right)  = \mathbf{x} \odot  \mathbf{b}$ (entry-wise product). Then ridge regression on the target task data(X, y), minimize $\mathop{\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}}\limits_{{\parallel \mathbf{w}\parallel  \leq  r}}\frac{1}{2{n}_{2}}\parallel X$ . $\operatorname{diag}\left( \mathbf{b}\right)  \cdot  \mathbf{w} - \mathbf{y}{\parallel }_{2}^{2}$ , is equivalent to $\mathop{\operatorname{minimize}}\limits_{{\parallel \operatorname{diag}{\left( \mathbf{b}\right) }^{-1}\mathbf{v}\parallel  \leq  r}}\frac{1}{2{n}_{2}}\parallel X\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{y}{\parallel }_{2}^{2}$ . From the above equation, we see that the features with large $\left| {b}_{i}\right|$ (those that were useful on the source tasks) will be more heavily used than the ones with small $\left| {b}_{i}\right|$ due to the reweighed ${\ell }_{2}$ constraint. Thus the important features are learned from the source tasks, and the coefficients are learned from the target task.

Remark 5.1 (The non-convex landscape). Although the optimization problem [10] is non-convex, its structure allows us to apply existing landscape analysis of matrix factorization problems (Haeffele et al. 2014) and to show that it has the nice properties of no strict saddles and no bad local minima. Therefore, randomly initialized gradient descent or perturbed gradient descent are guaranteed to converge to a global minimum of 10 (Ge et al. 2015; Lee et al. 2016; Jin et al. 2017).

## 6 NEURAL NETWORKS

In this section, we show that we can provably learn good representations in a neural network.

Consider a two-layer ReLU neural network ${f}_{B,\mathbf{w}}\left( \mathbf{x}\right)  = {\mathbf{w}}^{\top }{\left( {B}^{\top }\mathbf{x}\right) }_{ + }$ , where $\mathbf{w} \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{d}, B \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{{d}_{0} \times  d}$ and $\mathbf{x} \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{{d}_{0}}$ . Here ${\left( \cdot \right) }_{ + }$ is the ReLU activation ${\left( z\right) }_{ + } = \max \{ 0, z\}$ defined element-wise. Namely, we let the representation function class be $\Phi  = \left\{  {\mathbf{x} \rightarrow  {\left( {B}^{\top }\mathbf{x}\right) }_{ + } \mid  B \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{{d}_{0} \times  d}}\right\}$ . On the source tasks we use the square loss with weight decay regularizer: ${}^{6}$

$$
\left( {\widehat{B},\widehat{W}}\right)  \leftarrow  \mathop{\operatorname{argmin}}\limits_{\substack{{B \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{{d}_{0} \times  d},} \\  {W = \left\lbrack  {{\mathbf{w}}_{1},\cdots ,{\mathbf{w}}_{T}}\right\rbrack   \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{d \times  T}} }}\frac{1}{2{n}_{1}T}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{t = 1}}^{T}{\begin{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{y}}_{t} - {\left( {X}_{t}B\right) }_{ + }{\mathbf{w}}_{t}\end{Vmatrix}}^{2} + \frac{\lambda }{2}\parallel B{\parallel }_{F}^{2} + \frac{\lambda }{2}\parallel W{\parallel }_{F}^{2}. \tag{15}
$$

On the target task, we simply re-train the output layer while fixing the hidden layer weights:

$$
{\widehat{\mathbf{w}}}_{T + 1} \leftarrow  \underset{\parallel \mathbf{w}\parallel  \leq  r}{\arg \min }\frac{1}{2{n}_{2}}{\begin{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{y}}_{T + 1} - {\left( {X}_{T + 1}\widehat{B}\right) }_{ + }\mathbf{w}\end{Vmatrix}}^{2}. \tag{16}
$$

Assumption 6.1. All tasks share the same input distribution: ${p}_{1} = \cdots  = {p}_{T + 1} = p$ . We redefine $\sum$ to be the covariance operator of the feature induced by ReLU, i.e., it is a kernel defined by $\sum \left( {\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}\right)  = {\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbf{x} \sim  p}\left\lbrack  {{\left( {\mathbf{u}}^{\top }\mathbf{x}\right) }_{ + }{\left( {\mathbf{v}}^{\top }\mathbf{x}\right) }_{ + }}\right\rbrack$ , for $\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}$ on the unit sphere ${\mathbb{S}}^{{d}_{0} - 1} \subset  {\mathbb{R}}^{{d}_{0}}$ .

Assumption 6.2 (teacher network). Assume for the source tasks that ${\mathbf{y}}_{t} = {\left( {X}_{t}{B}^{ * }\right) }_{ + }{\mathbf{w}}_{t}^{ * } + {\mathbf{z}}_{t}$ is generated by a teacher network with parameters ${B}^{ * } \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{{d}_{0} \times  d},{W}^{ * } = \left\lbrack  {{\mathbf{w}}_{1}^{ * },\cdots ,{\mathbf{w}}_{T}^{ * }}\right\rbrack   \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{d \times  T}$ , and noise term ${\mathbf{z}}_{t} \sim  \mathcal{N}\left( {0,{\sigma }^{2}I}\right)$ . Similarly for the target task ${\mathbf{y}}_{T + 1} = {\left( {X}_{T + 1}{B}_{T + 1}^{ * }\right) }_{ + }{\mathbf{w}}_{T + 1}^{ * } + {\mathbf{z}}_{T + 1}$ where ${\mathbf{z}}_{T + 1} \sim  \mathcal{N}\left( {0,{\sigma }^{2}I}\right)$ . Let $\nu  = \mathcal{N}\left( {0,{B}^{ * }{W}^{ * }{\left( {W}^{ * }\right) }^{\top }{\left( {B}^{ * }\right) }^{\top }/T}\right)$ .

Theorem 6.1. Fix a failure probability $\delta  \in  \left( {0,1}\right)$ . Under Assumptions 4.1 6.1 and 6.2 we further assume ${n}_{1} \gg  {\rho }^{4}T{\bar{R}}^{2}{\sigma }^{2}\operatorname{Tr}\left( \sum \right) \log \left( {1/\delta }\right) ,{n}_{2} \gg  {\rho }^{4}{\sigma }^{2}{\bar{R}}^{2}\parallel \sum \parallel \log \left( {1/\delta }\right)$ and $\overline{{n}_{1}} \geq  {n}_{2}$ , where $\bar{R} =$ $\left( {\frac{1}{2}{\begin{Vmatrix}{B}^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}_{F}^{2} + \frac{1}{2}{\begin{Vmatrix}{W}^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}_{F}^{2}}\right) /\sqrt{T}$ . Let the target task model be coherent with the source task models in the sense that ${B}_{T + 1}^{ * }{\mathbf{w}}_{T + 1}^{ * } \sim  \nu$ . Set ${r}^{2} = 2\left( {{\begin{Vmatrix}{B}^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}_{F}^{2} + {\begin{Vmatrix}{W}^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}_{F}^{2}}\right) /T$ and $\lambda  = \Theta \left( {\frac{1}{\sqrt{{n}_{1}}}{\left( \log 1/\delta \right) }^{2/3}}\right.$ . $\left. {\left( {\sqrt{T\parallel \sum {\parallel }_{2}} + \sqrt{\operatorname{Tr}\left( \sum \right) }}\right) \log \left( {n + T}\right) }\right)$ . Then with probability at least $1 - \delta$ over the samples, the expected excess risk of the learned predictor $\mathbf{x} \mapsto  {\widehat{\mathbf{w}}}_{T + 1}^{\top }{\left( {\widehat{B}}^{\top }\mathbf{x}\right) }_{ + }$ on the target task satisfies:

$$
{\mathbb{E}}_{{B}_{T + 1}^{ * }{\mathbf{w}}_{T + 1}^{ * } \sim  \nu }\left\lbrack  {\operatorname{ER}\left( {f}_{\widehat{B},{\widehat{\mathbf{w}}}_{T + 1}}\right) }\right\rbrack   \leq  \sigma \bar{R} \cdot  \widetilde{O}\left( {\frac{\sqrt{\operatorname{Tr}\left( \sum \right) }}{\sqrt{{n}_{1}T}} + \frac{\sqrt{\parallel \sum {\parallel }_{2}}}{\sqrt{{n}_{2}}}}\right) . \tag{17}
$$

To highlight the advantage of representation learning, we compare to training a neural network with weight decay directly on the target task:

$$
\left( {\widehat{B},\widehat{\mathbf{w}}}\right)  = \underset{B,\mathbf{w}}{\arg \min }\frac{1}{2n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{\begin{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{y}}_{t + 1} - {\left( {X}_{T + 1}B\right) }_{ + }\mathbf{w}\end{Vmatrix}}^{2} + \frac{\lambda }{2}\parallel B{\parallel }_{F}^{2} + \frac{\lambda }{2}\parallel \mathbf{w}{\parallel }_{2}^{2}. \tag{18}
$$

The error of the baseline method is

$$
\mathbb{E}\left\lbrack  {\operatorname{ER}\left( {f}_{\widehat{B},\widehat{\mathbf{w}}}\right) }\right\rbrack   \lesssim  \sigma \bar{R}\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Tr}\left( \sum \right) }{{n}_{2}}}. \tag{19}
$$

We see that Equation (17) is always smaller than Equation (19) since ${n}_{1}T \geq  {n}_{2}$ . See Appendix D for the proof of Theorem 6.1 and the calculation of (19).

## 7 CONCLUSION

We gave the first statistical analysis showing that representation learning can fully exploit all data points from source tasks to enable few-shot learning on a target task. This type of results were shown for both low-dimensional and high-dimensional representation function classes.

There are many important directions to pursue in representation learning and few-shot learning. Our results in Sections 5 and 6 indicate that explicit low dimensionality is not necessary, and norm-based capacity control also forces the classifier to learn good representations. Further questions include whether this is a general phenomenon in all deep learning models, whether other capacity control can be applied, and how to optimize to attain good representations.

---

${}^{6}$ Wei et al. (2019) show that (15) can be minimized in polynomial iteration complexity using perturbed gradient descent, though potentially exponential width is required.

## Summary 

The paper describes excess risk bounds for ERM in the few-shot learning setting where one has access to $n_1$ samples from each of the $T$ source tasks and $n_2$ samples from the target class. Under the assumption that there exists a ground-truth representation map, shared across all tasks, and a ground-truth task-specific linear map, that maps from the representation space to output space, the authors derive bounds that make use of all $n_1T$ data samples from the source tasks to bound the excess risk of the ERM.  

The bounds that are derived are for the following three settings: 1) low dimensional linear representation, 2) general linear map with $\ell$-2 norm-based capacity control for the representation, and 3) linear map with a Relu non-linearity based representation. The key innovation is the structure imparted onto the input distribution of the source and target tasks where the assumption is that the input distribution of *all* the tasks covers the target task. The assumptions get progressively stricter for each of the three cases where for the low dimensional linear case, the assumption is that covariance of the target tsk is dominated by the covariance of all the source tasks, for the high dimensional case, the mean covariance is shared across tasks and finally for the neural network cases where the tasks share the same input distribution. These assumptions allow the improvement of the bound in Maurer et al. 2016. 


## Strengths: 

1. Overall the paper is well written and motivated. The implication of the results are well discussed and makes for a good read. 
2. Under the assumptions on input distribution, results are an improvement over the iid task case and provides theoretical motivation for few-shot learning. 
3. Generalizes the Excess risk bound for the ERM in [1] for the low dimensional linear and the high dimensional linear setting. Extends the result to the ERM of 2 layer Relu network. 

## Weaknesses

1. The bound is valid when one has access to oracle ERM. This is not the case for most non-convex optimization. Especially in the case of the neural network extension.
2. As pointed out by the authors, many results are very similar to concurrent work of [1]
3. The paper lacks discussion with some prior work  [2] where the authors obtained results for task averaged excess risk. The result in this work is not for new task but since the authors make strong assumptions on input data distribution and task model the result seems like a natural extension of the results in [1].

## Discussion and concerns

Both Theorem 5.1 and 6.1 make the coherence assumption on the target task model. I understand that it allows us to get a bound in terms of $\| \Theta^*\|$ but the implications of this assumption is not well discussed in the paper. This looks like assumption 4.3 for Theorem 4.1. Any understanding of how the results would change if we don’t make the assumption 4.3 and the coherence assumptions?


__EDIT: Added references__
[1] Nilesh Tripuraneni, Chi Jin, and Michael I Jordan. Provable meta-learning of linear representations. arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.11684, 2020
[2] Pontil, M., & Maurer, A. (2013, June). Excess risk bounds for multitask learning with trace norm regularization. In Conference on Learning Theory (pp. 55-76).
